subject: BRGSA
subjectTitle: Business Research and Growth Systems Architecture

sections.rule: One correct option. Two marks each. No negative marking.
A short scenario, then a task. Both parts must be right for the marks. No partial credit.
A complete structured response. Not machine-marked.

paper.stem: A useful pricing change genuinely improves conversion, but an underpowered test concludes that nothing changed. Which error is this?
options: A Type I error, a false positive
No error because the result was not significant
Survivorship bias alone, with no testing error involved
A Type II error, a false negative

paper.caselet: A team spends ₹2,00,000 on a paid channel. Their average contract value is ₹1,000 a month and their acquisition cost on that channel lands near ₹8,000.
paper.stem: What should the team do?
options: Stop the channel on price-point mismatch, because that arithmetic is settled before any creative decision is taken.
Keep the channel and raise the price, since a contract worth more would make the same acquisition cost acceptable.
Improve the creative and the targeting first, since a high acquisition cost usually reflects a weak campaign rather than the channel.
Continue for a full quarter, because paid channels need time before their true cost per customer can be judged.

paper.stem: A test declares a new onboarding flow better when there is actually no real improvement. Which error occurred?
options: Cohort decay, where a group's behaviour drifts across the whole measurement period afterwards
A sampling frame problem, where the wrong population was measured from the start
Type II: a false negative, missing a real effect that was actually there
Type I: a false positive, declaring an effect that is not there

paper.stem: For an A/B landing-page test, which plain-language null hypothesis is best formed?
options: There is never a meaningful difference between A and B until the evidence is strong enough to reject that position
Both variants must receive an identical number of conversions before the test result can be considered valid at all
Variant B will definitely win once enough traffic has been sent through both of the pages being compared
The team prefers Variant A and should state that preference before the test begins

paper.caselet: Two companies each average $10,000 in annual revenue per account. One charges a flat rate; the other charges per seat. A year later the second has grown revenue per account substantially and the first has not, with no change in either customer base.
paper.stem: What explains the difference?
options: The per-seat company raised its list price during the year, which the flat-rate company chose not to do.
The structures make different promises about growth: per-seat revenue grows as a customer's team grows, flat rate does not.
The per-seat company's customers were larger organisations to begin with, so the same structure produced more revenue from each of them.
The flat-rate company has better retention, which it bought by holding its price steady through the year.

paper.stem: A team spends ₹3,00,000 on a channel and acquires 120 paying customers attributable to it. What is channel CAC?
A retention curve falls sharply, then settles into a stable plateau. What is the most useful interpretation?
options: Acquisition cost must therefore be close to zero for this product to work
Every user will eventually churn no matter what the product does
The product should be scaled immediately, regardless of what the unit economics say
Early activation is weak, but the curve flattens, so a retained core always finds durable value

paper.stem: For a team-based B2B SaaS product, which retention unit is usually more decision-useful than counting individual logins alone?
options: The count of social media followers
The paying account or team
The total number of website visitors
Every employee working in the addressable market

paper.stem: An early startup has no repeatable channel and uncertain retention. Which move fits its stage?
options: Maximise automation everywhere before making direct customer contact
Optimise quarterly media efficiency at scale across paid channels
Build a large specialist growth organisation immediately
Run founder-close, high-learning tests to find repeatability

paper.stem: A channel reaches the ICP precisely but takes 14 months to yield results; the startup has three months of runway. Which channel-fit property fails most directly?
options: The precision of its targeting
Product desirability itself, by the course's own definition of it
The clarity of the message being sent out alone
Time to result relative to the business constraint

paper.stem: Which change most clearly turns cold email activity into an outbound system?
options: Defining ICP, list quality, sequence and qualification as one repeatable flow, never as separate tactics
Counting every single email open as a genuine sales opportunity worth adding to the pipeline
Sending a much larger volume of the same generic messages out to everyone every single week
Changing the email copy every single day without ever stating a hypothesis to test first

paper.caselet: Paid traffic converts, but new users fail activation and churn. Marketing hits its lead target; product ships features; neither owns the transition.
paper.stem: What would a growth diagnosis do first?
options: Rename the marketing team as the growth team
Buy substantially more paid traffic
Own the cross-functional activation/retention transition and define one shared constraint metric
Celebrate that both teams hit their targets

paper.stem: Which pairing best fits the course's early customer-acquisition logic?
options: Both: nationwide paid acquisition at full scale from day one
B2B: mass television advertising from day one; B2C: one-to-one enterprise demonstrations
B2B: focused founder-led sales; B2C: concentrated cohort launch with seeding, proof, and repurchase
Both: wait for organic search traffic to arrive on its own

paper.caselet: Monthly active users rose from 10,000 to 14,000 after a large campaign. Each new signup cohort, however, retains fewer users by week four than the cohort before it.
paper.stem: What does the cohort view reveal?
options: Acquisition volume is masking deteriorating retention
Retention is improving because the total user number is larger
The campaign has proven that product-market fit exists
Cohorts cannot meaningfully be compared across time

paper.stem: Why is ‘Would you buy this?’ a weak primary validation question?
options: People cannot understand a product before launch
Stated intention under social pressure never reliably predicts actual purchase behaviour
Surveys always require more than a thousand responses before they mean anything
Only direct competitors are allowed to run such surveys

paper.caselet: A complex enterprise product needs security review, multi-stakeholder approval, custom integration, and a high annual contract.
paper.stem: Which primary motion is better matched?
options: Pure self-serve PLG with no human support
Sales-led growth supported by product experience
No deliberate acquisition motion of any kind
Consumer referral coupons only

paper.caselet: A funnel runs 10,000 visitors, 1,200 signups, 400 activations and 30 paying customers.
paper.stem: Where is the constraint?
options: Signup to activation at 33%, since only the slowest stage sets the pace and effort on any other adds nothing.
Visitor to signup, where 8,800 people are lost — by far the largest fall anywhere in the funnel.
Nowhere yet, because a funnel with four stages needs a much longer observation window before any constraint in it can fairly be named.
Activation to paid, at 7.5%, which is the lowest conversion rate of the three stages shown.

paper.caselet: An activation test reaches its pre-set sample. Variant B moves the named activation metric from 34% to 39%, inside the pre-registered iterate band of 37–42%. Revenue has not matured yet.
paper.stem: What should the team do?
options: Iterate according to the rule and continue tracking the defensible downstream link
Ignore the named activation metric entirely and use the total click count instead
Call Variant B the winner because the number improved in the test run
Move the scale threshold down to 39% after seeing how the result landed

paper.caselet: An experiment hypothesised activation moving from 34% to 45%. It lands at 38%, and the team wants to keep iterating.
paper.stem: What settles whether to continue?
options: The thresholds written before the experiment went live, since all four parts of the rule are agreed in advance.
Whether the team has capacity, since a live experiment that is improving the number is worth keeping while resources allow.
Whether 38% is a statistically significant improvement over 34%, which is what decides if the effect is real.
Whether another variation could plausibly close the remaining gap, which is the test for a worthwhile iteration.

paper.stem: Which view best helps locate when and for whom churn occurs?
options: Cohort retention and time-to-churn together, always segmented by the relevant customer unit
The total number of emails ever sent
The all-time cumulative count of customers acquired
The total quarterly advertising impressions delivered across all channels

paper.caselet: A channel reaches the intended buyer precisely but takes fourteen months to produce revenue, and the company has three months of runway.
paper.stem: Fill both parts of the recommendation so the action and framework agree.

blanks.label: Choose the decision
options: The product clearly cannot have found product-market fit yet. (Channel fit)
All B2B products require television advertising in order to reach the relevant decision-makers at scale. (Channel fit)
The high view count is proof enough that the channel is working exactly as intended. (Channel fit)
Score candidate channels against the product's economics and timing constraints before spending, and reject one that fails any single dimension. (Channel fit)

blanks.label: Choose the framework
options: Channel fit: Demand signals sit on a commitment spectrum: social engagement is the easiest to produce and the least meaningful, while a payment or signed commitment is a different category of evidence altogether.
Channel fit: Activation is the first observable moment a user experiences the promised value, and every step standing between signup and that moment sheds a share of the users still remaining.
Channel fit: Lean validation asks whether real people will take a real action on a real offer, and answers it before the product is built at a fraction of the cost of building it.

Channel fit: Every channel has fixed properties — targeting, control, input cost, output quality, time to result and economics — and it fits only when those match the product's buyer and unit economics.

paper.caselet: Two hundred people say they like the idea, thirty join a wait-list, and four accept a refundable deposit under stated terms. The founder wants to report the survey as the strongest demand signal.
paper.stem: Fill both parts of the recommendation so the action and framework agree.

blanks.label: Choose the decision
options: Apply the joining test — does one more user make the product more valuable to existing users — and run the referral playbook when the answer is no. (Pre-sales commitment and evidence strength)
‘A great idea’ in a survey. (Pre-sales commitment and evidence strength)
A like on the announcement. (Pre-sales commitment and evidence strength)
Weight every demand signal by what it cost the prospect to give, and require a real commitment before treating demand as proven. (Pre-sales commitment and evidence strength)

blanks.label: Choose the framework
options: Pre-sales commitment and evidence strength: A Type I error scales something that does not work; a Type II error abandons something that does. Every test outcome lands in one of the four cells of that matrix.

Pre-sales commitment and evidence strength: Lean validation asks whether real people will take a real action on a real offer, and answers it before the product is built at a fraction of the cost of building it.

Pre-sales commitment and evidence strength: An experiment starts from the null position that nothing changed, and the variant earns the decision only when evidence collected to a pre-set sample is strong enough to reject it.

Pre-sales commitment and evidence strength: Demand signals sit on a commitment spectrum: social engagement is the easiest to produce and the least meaningful, while a payment or signed commitment is a different category of evidence altogether.

paper.caselet: Total active users climb every month while each newer signup cohort holds fewer users at week four than the cohort before it, and the team plans to increase spend.
paper.stem: Fill both parts of the recommendation so the action and framework agree.

blanks.label: Choose the decision
options: Apply the joining test — does one more user make the product more valuable to existing users — and run the referral playbook when the answer is no. (Cohorts and retention)
Retention is improving because the total user number is larger. (Cohorts and retention)
The campaign has proven that product-market fit exists. (Cohorts and retention)
Read retention by signup cohort and time since entry before concluding from a rising total that growth is working. (Cohorts and retention)

blanks.label: Choose the framework
options: Cohorts and retention: Demand signals sit on a commitment spectrum: social engagement is the easiest to produce and the least meaningful, while a payment or signed commitment is a different category of evidence altogether.
Cohorts and retention: A cohort groups users by when they entered so retention can be compared at equal age, which aggregate totals cannot do because they mix new arrivals with survivors.
Cohorts and retention: CAC carries no decision meaning without an estimate of the value it buys, so LTV is estimated early from observed lifespan, margin and revenue rather than waited for.
Cohorts and retention: Lean validation asks whether real people will take a real action on a real offer, and answers it before the product is built at a fraction of the cost of building it.

paper.caselet: A subscription loses some accounts while retained customers expand enough that recurring revenue still rises; the team reports only logo churn and plans more acquisition.
paper.stem: Fill both parts of the recommendation so the action and framework agree.

blanks.label: Choose the decision
options: NRR is 125%, so the revenue base is compounding. (Pricing structure and NRR)
Design the pricing structure around the expansion behaviour the business needs, and read NRR on the existing cohort before crediting growth to it. (Pricing structure and NRR)
Apply the joining test — does one more user make the product more valuable to existing users — and run the referral playbook when the answer is no. (Pricing structure and NRR)
NRR cannot be calculated without new sales figures. (Pricing structure and NRR)

blanks.label: Choose the framework
options: Pricing structure and NRR: Demand signals sit on a commitment spectrum: social engagement is the easiest to produce and the least meaningful, while a payment or signed commitment is a different category of evidence altogether.
Pricing structure and NRR: Lean validation asks whether real people will take a real action on a real offer, and answers it before the product is built at a fraction of the cost of building it.

Pricing structure and NRR: Pricing is a structure rather than a number: tiers, units, limits and packaging decide how customers enter, upgrade and expand, and NRR measures whether the existing base grows without counting new customers.

Pricing structure and NRR: Revenue crosses several team handoffs, and each needs an entry criterion, an owner, the context that must travel with it and a response-time SLA; payback measures how long acquisition cash stays tied up before gross profit returns it.

paper.caselet: A fleet-tracking company has capacity for six engineering projects this quarter and forty candidate ideas. The chief executive is pressing for a public API, which is highly visible, carries an eight-week estimate, has been requested by two prospects and no existing customer, and has no identified effect on any current metric. A second candidate, a two-week change collapsing a six-step vehicle-onboarding flow to two steps, is supported by session recordings of nineteen customers abandoning at step four; the company's own data shows fleets that finish onboarding within seven days renew at three times the rate of those that do not, and 41% currently finish inside seven days. A third would rebuild the marketing-to-sales handoff, where 210 qualified leads produced 96 accepted, the definition of the remaining 114 has never been agreed between the two teams, and first contact averages six days. Nobody at the company has spoken to a churned customer in eleven months; the head of product declined a proposed round of interviews as anecdotal. Ideas are currently ranked in a spreadsheet by a single enthusiasm score contributed by whoever proposed them.
paper.stem: Write the recommendation for how this quarter's six slots should be decided, and what should be in them. Deal with the chief executive's proposal explicitly.

paper.caselet: A direct-to-consumer coffee brand sells a ₹1,150 monthly subscription. To arrest a decline it ran a 30% launch discount for first-time subscribers. Signups rose 240% during the eight-week offer and the growth lead has proposed making the discount permanent, citing contribution margin that stayed positive throughout. The cohort numbers were not in that proposal. Discounted subscribers cancel at 58% by month three against 21% for full-price subscribers, and 4% ever accept the price increase at renewal. Blended acquisition cost is ₹1,900. Full-price subscribers contribute about ₹430 a month against ₹180 for discounted ones. Separately the team has a backlog of eleven ideas and capacity for three: the permanent discount, a ₹1,900 twin-bag tier that 340 customers have asked for by email, and a packaging redesign the founder favours which no customer has mentioned and which would take nine weeks. There is no tier above the single plan today.
paper.stem: Write the recommendation on the discount and on which three ideas should be built. Say plainly what the signup figure did and did not demonstrate.
